topic_and_scope: Systematic assessment of spina bifida epidemiology and morbidity in Hispanic Americans, focusing on prevalence, risk factors, and the health and economic burden, with an emphasis on gaps in standardization, representation, and translation into prevention and policy.
main_themes: Disparities in prevalence and morbidity of spina bifida in Hispanic Americans compared with non-Hispanic White individuals
Multifactorial risk determinants including socioeconomic status, immigration/acculturation, environmental exposures, and clinical factors
Need for standardized reporting, representative research, and actionable, culturally tailored prevention and treatment strategies
main_findings: Hispanic Americans show higher birth prevalence of spina bifida per 10,000 births and higher morbidity burden compared with NHW in multiple studies, with the disparity persisting after folic acid fortification efforts.

Folate fortification reduced spina bifida prevalence overall but did not fully eliminate the disparity; substantial heterogeneity across studies suggests differences in time periods, geography, reporting, and population characteristics, highlighting gaps in standardized measurement and reporting

key_gaps.description: Lack of standardized reporting guidelines and core data elements for prevalence, risk factors, and morbidity of spina bifida in Hispanic American populations across studies

Underrepresentation of Hispanic Americans in prevention and treatment research, including prenatal repair trials, and insufficient understanding of acculturation-, immigration-, and health-system-related determinants driving disparities

future_directions.title: Develop and adopt standardized reporting guidelines for spina bifida epidemiology in Hispanic Americans
future_directions.rationale: The reviewed literature shows high heterogeneity due to differences in timeframes, locations, and reporting. Establishing core data elements (prevalence per 10,000 births, fortification status, exposure categories, morbidity outcomes, and health-related quality of life metrics) and uniform case definitions will enable valid cross-study comparisons and meta-analyses. Steps include forming a multidisciplinary consensus panel, publishing a minimal dataset, and embedding these standards in future regional registries and national databases.

future_directions.title: Initiate prospective multicenter cohort studies in diverse Hispanic American populations
future_directions.rationale: Most existing studies are retrospective and heterogeneous, limiting causal inference. Prospective cohorts should systematically collect preconception and prenatal data on SES, nativity/acculturation, language, health literacy, nutrition (folate intake), diabetes/obesity, environmental exposures, and access to care. A diverse geographic mix (e.g., Southwest, Texas-Mouth border, California, Florida) will improve generalizability and help disentangle contextual factors driving disparities. Integrate linkage to SB outcomes to quantify prevention and treatment effects over time.

future_directions.title: Evaluate and optimize folic acid fortification strategies targeting traditional Hispanic diets
future_directions.rationale: Fortification reduced SB prevalence but disparities persist, suggesting inadequate reach or impact in Hispanic subgroups. Research should assess uptake of current fortification policies (including corn masa fortification) and explore additional strategies (e.g., fortification of salt or other staples) with careful monitoring of folate biomarkers and birth outcomes. Actionable next steps include natural experiments, policy analysis, and community-based trials to measure population-level impact on SB incidence and disparities.

future_directions.title: Implement culturally tailored health literacy and prenatal care access programs
future_directions.rationale: Low education levels, language barriers, and health literacy gaps are repeatedly associated with higher SB risk and reduced access to preventive care. Develop bilingual, culturally appropriate educational materials and navigation supports; test their effectiveness in improving knowledge, prenatal care initiation, and adherence to preventive measures. Use pragmatic trial designs in high-risk communities and assess SB-related outcomes and quality of care indicators.

future_directions.title: Investigate barriers to prenatal surgical repair and increase access for Hispanic Americans
future_directions.rationale: Prenatal repair (fetal surgery) shows improved outcomes but Hispanic representation is low, with uptake limited by insurance, travel costs, eligibility criteria, and obesity. Conduct qualitative studies to map barriers, policy analyses to identify systemic obstacles, and pilot programs offering travel subsidies, insurance navigation, and culturally competent counseling. Evaluate whether reducing barriers increases prenatal repair uptake and improves neonatal and long-term outcomes.

future_directions.title: Map environmental exposure pathways and quantify toxicant-related SB risk in Hispanic communities
future_directions.rationale: Evidence links proximity to cultivated fields and pesticide exposure with SB risk; robust exposure assessment is needed. Combine geographic information systems, environmental sampling, and biomonitoring to model dose–response relationships while adjusting for SES and other confounders. The goal is to identify modifiable environmental factors and guide regulatory and community mitigation efforts.

future_directions.title: quantify lifetime economic burden and health-related quality of life in Hispanic SB cohorts to inform policy
future_directions.rationale: SB imposes substantial direct and indirect costs and reduced HRQoL, particularly in low-SES Hispanic populations. Prospective cost-of-illness studies and HRQoL assessments should be conducted within SB cohorts to generate precise, region-specific data. Use these data to advocate for policy changes, insurance coverage improvements, and allocation of resources for prevention, early intervention, and caregiver support.
